passages.t: ‘Our Lord is above all gods’: a hymn made of older hymns
passages.happening:
Psalm 135 opens and closes with “Hallelujah!” It calls the temple servants to praise. “Give praise, O servants of the LORD, who stand in the house of the LORD” (verses 1 and 2). “Hallelujah, for the LORD is good; sing praises to His name, for it is lovely” (verse 3).

It gives reasons. God chose Israel “as His treasured possession” (verse 4). “For I know that the LORD is great; our Lord is above all gods” (verse 5). He does what he pleases in heaven, earth and sea (verse 6). He raises the clouds and sends lightning, rain and wind (verse 7).

Then the psalm tells Israel's story in brief: the firstborn of Egypt struck down (verse 8), signs against Pharaoh (verse 9), kings defeated, “Sihon king of the Amorites, Og king of Bashan” (verse 11), and the land given to Israel (verse 12). “Your name, O LORD, endures forever” (verse 13).

The idols get the same scorn as in Psalm 115: silver and gold with mouths that cannot speak (verses 15 to 18). And it ends with every group in the temple called to bless the LORD: Israel, Aaron, Levi, and all who fear him (verses 19 and 20).
passages.hearers:
A first hearer who knew the older Scriptures would hear many of them here. Verses 15 to 18 are nearly the same as Psalm 115:4-8. Verse 7 matches Jeremiah: “He causes the clouds to rise from the ends of the earth. He generates the lightning with the rain and brings forth the wind from His storehouses” (Jeremiah 10:13). Verse 14 repeats the Song of Moses: “For the LORD will vindicate His people and have compassion on His servants” (Deuteronomy 32:36). ‘Treasured possession’ is what God called Israel at Mount Sinai (Exodus 19:5). Many scholars think a temple singer after the exile wove these older lines together. Others note that words shared in worship could be used for a long time.

Verse 7 has an edge. Israel's Canaanite neighbours gave the credit for storms and rain to Baal. The psalm gives all of it to the LORD.

Sihon and Og were kings east of the Jordan who would not let Israel pass, and came out to fight (Numbers 21:23-24). The note on Psalm 136 meets them again.

‘The house of Levi’ in verse 20 is new. Psalms 115 and 118 named Israel, Aaron and those who fear the LORD. Here the Levites, the temple's helpers and singers, are named too.
passages.later:
Peter wrote to the church in words that echo verse 4: “But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God's own possession” (1 Peter 2:9).

Jesus said the Father “sends rain on the righteous and the unrighteous” (Matthew 5:45). Paul told the people of Lystra that God “gives you rain from heaven and fruitful seasons” (Acts 14:17).
passages.hard: Verses 10 to 12 praise God for striking down kings and nations. The note on Psalm 106 sets out how Christians read Israel's conquest stories, and the note on Psalm 136 adds a word more. No reading of these verses gives anyone today a right to harm another person or people.
passages.asks:
Psalm 135 is made of borrowed words, and that is part of its lesson. Praise does not have to be new to be true. The old words of Scripture can become your own.

Verse 5 says, ‘I know that the LORD is great.’ What do you know about God, from his word and from your own life? Say it out loud, as this singer did.
